items.prose: A share moves up £1, stays flat, or moves down £1 on each of three days. An outcome is the list of three moves, such as up, flat, down.
items.question: How many of the outcomes leave the share where it started?

widget.label: Outcomes ending where it started
widget.accept: 7 exactly: flat, flat, flat, plus the 6 orders of up, flat and down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The moves must cancel: list every way, in every order.

byKey.flat-only: Flat three times is one way. One up, one down and one flat also cancel, in any order.
byKey.no-flat: You found the 6 orders of up, flat and down. Flat, flat, flat also ends where it started.
byKey.one-order: You counted each mix once. Up, flat, down and down, flat, up are different paths.

explain.text: The moves must sum to 0. Either all three are flat, 1 way, or there is one up, one down and one flat, in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ orders. That is 7 of the $3^3 = 27$ outcomes.

items.question: What is $P(\text{the larger number is } 4)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count rolls with both dice at most 4, then take away those with both at most 3.

byKey.double: You counted (4, 4) twice, once as each die.
byKey.one-die: That is one die showing 4. The other die must also be 4 or less.
byKey.at-most: That is the chance the larger is at most 4. Take away the 9 rolls with both dice at most 3.

explain.text: Both dice at most 4 gives $4^2 = 16$ rolls, and both at most 3 gives $3^2 = 9$. The larger is exactly 4 in $16 - 9 = 7$ rolls. So $P = \tfrac{7}{36}$.

items.prose: A bet pays £18 if two fair dice show a double, and nothing otherwise. Sam prices it with his list of 21 unordered pairs, 6 of them doubles.
items.question: What is the fair price, the average payout per roll, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the doubles among the 36 equally likely rolls.

byKey.sam: You used Sam's 21 pairs. A double is one roll but a mixed pair is two, so his pairs are not equally likely.
byKey.one: You counted one double. There are six: (1, 1) to (6, 6).
byKey.half: You split into double or not. Only 6 of the 36 rolls are doubles.

explain.text: Six of the 36 equally likely rolls are doubles. Over 36 rolls the bet pays $6 \times \text{£}18 = \text{£}108$, which is £3.00 a roll. Sam's $\tfrac{6}{21}$ would price it at about £5.14, far too high.

items.prose: Three events on one trading day. $A$: the momentum signal fires. $B$: the value signal fires. $C$: volatility is high.
items.question: Tap every region of $(A \cup B) \cap C^c$: at least one signal fires on a calm day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade $A \cup B$ first, then remove everything inside $C$.

byKey.with-c: You shaded all of $A \cup B$. The regions inside $C$ are high-volatility days, so remove them.
byKey.xor: You missed the region where both signals fire on a calm day. “Or” includes both.
byKey.c-part: That is $(A \cup B) \cap C$, the volatile days. We want the calm ones.

explain.text: $A \cup B$ is every region inside the $A$ or $B$ circles. Intersecting with $C^c$ keeps only the parts outside $C$. That leaves $A$ only, $B$ only, and $A$ and $B$ without $C$.

items.prose: $A$ and $B$ are events in the same sample space.
items.question: Which sets equal $A^c \cup B^c$? Select all that apply.

options.why: That is neither event, only the outside region. $A^c \cup B^c$ also holds $A$ only and $B$ only.
That is neither event again. A complement turns a union into an intersection, not into a union.

feedback.correct: Both name “not both”: everything outside the overlap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade $A^c$ and $B^c$, then take every region in at least one.

explain.text: $A^c \cup B^c$ holds every outcome missing $A$ or missing $B$, so everything but the overlap. That is $(A \cap B)^c$ by De Morgan. Listing the three regions outside the overlap gives the second set.

items.prose: Each limit order you place fills with chance 0.2, independently of the others. You want at least one fill with chance 0.95 or more.
items.question: What is the smallest number of orders that does it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $n$ with $0.8^n \le 0.05$.

byKey.adding: You added 0.2 per order until you passed 0.95. Five orders give only $1 - 0.8^5 \approx 0.672$.
byKey.thirteen: Close: $0.8^{13} \approx 0.0550$, so 13 orders give about 0.945. One more is needed.

items.prose: A desk runs three independent strategies. Each has a losing month with chance 0.25, 0.3 and 0.4 respectively.
items.question: What is the chance at least one strategy has a losing month? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance all three avoid a loss, then take it from 1.

byKey.adding: You added the three chances. Months where two strategies lose are counted twice.
byKey.all: That is $0.25 \times 0.3 \times 0.4$, all three losing together.
byKey.none: That is the chance no strategy loses. Take it from 1.

explain.text: No losing month needs all three to avoid a loss: $0.75 \times 0.7 \times 0.6 = 0.315$. So at least one loses with chance $1 - 0.315 = 0.685$. Each chance of no loss differs, so the product has three different factors.

items.title: At least one double six
items.prose: We want $P(\text{at least one double six in } n \text{ rolls of two dice})$.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: One roll of two dice has 36 equally likely outcomes, and 35 of them are not a double six.
$n$ rolls have $36^n$ equally likely outcomes, and $35^n$ of them contain no double six.
At least one double six is the complement of none: $P = 1 - \left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^n$.

feedback.correct: Count one roll, count $n$ rolls, divide, then take the complement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with a single roll and build up to $n$ rolls before the complement.

explain.text: The choices multiply across rolls, giving $36^n$ outcomes and $35^n$ without a double six. Dividing gives $P(\text{none})$. The complement rule finishes it.

items.title: The Chevalier de Méré's two bets
items.prompt:
In the 1650s the Chevalier de Méré made two even-money bets. Bet 1: at least one six in 4 rolls of a fair die. Bet 2: at least one double six in 24 rolls of two fair dice. He reasoned that both win with chance $4 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 24 \times \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{2}{3}$, yet he lost money on bet 2.

(a) Find the exact chance of winning bet 1, by counting outcomes. Does it win in the long run?

(b) Find the chance of winning bet 2, to 4 decimal places. Does it win in the long run?

(c) Explain what is wrong with his reasoning. Use a count to show it.

(d) Find the smallest number of rolls that makes bet 2 favourable.
items.model:
**(a)** Four rolls of a die have $6^4 = 1296$ equally likely outcomes. An outcome with no six uses one of 5 faces on each roll, so $5^4 = 625$ outcomes have no six. “At least one six” is the complement of “no six”, so
$$P(\text{win bet 1}) = 1 - \frac{625}{1296} = \frac{671}{1296} \approx 0.5177.$$
This is above $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so the even-money bet wins in the long run.

**(b)** One roll of two dice has 36 equally likely outcomes, and 35 are not a double six. So 24 rolls have $36^{24}$ outcomes, $35^{24}$ of them with no double six:
$$P(\text{win bet 2}) = 1 - \left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^{24} \approx 1 - 0.5086 = 0.4914.$$
This is below $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so bet 2 loses in the long run.

**(c)** Adding $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll adds the chances of four overlapping events, “six on roll $i$”. An outcome with two or more sixes lies in several of them, so it is counted more than once. In counts: each event holds $6^3 = 216$ outcomes, and $4 \times 216 = 864$. But only 671 distinct outcomes contain a six, so 193 counts are repeats. The added number is not even a probability: with 7 rolls it would be $\tfrac{7}{6} > 1$.

**(d)** We need $1 - \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^n > \tfrac{1}{2}$, so $\left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^n < \tfrac{1}{2}$. Taking logs, $n > \tfrac{\ln 0.5}{\ln(35/36)} \approx 24.6$. So $n = 25$: $1 - \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{25} \approx 0.5055$, while 24 rolls give 0.4914.

rubric.text: Counts $6^4 = 1296$ outcomes and $5^4 = 625$ with no six, and uses the complement.
Reaches $\tfrac{671}{1296} \approx 0.5177$ and says bet 1 wins in the long run.
Uses $P(\text{no double six}) = \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{24}$ with a reason (35 of 36 outcomes per roll).
Reaches about 0.4914 and says bet 2 loses in the long run.
Explains that adding counts outcomes with several sixes more than once, with a count (864 against 671) or the sum passing 1.
Finds $n = 25$ and checks both 24 and 25 rolls.
